The parts that matter are the publisher, created with a topic name and a history depth; the timer, whose callback builds and publishes a message; the members that keep both alive; and
, without which the timer never fires. You pass if you had all four and the structure would compile with small fixes. Missing
or the members is a partial pass, and more than that is a fail. A plain
for the depth, a constructor without
all pass too; the theory below says why this page writes each of them differently.
A topic is a named channel that carries exactly one message type, such as
. Any number of nodes can publish to it and any number can subscribe, and each message type is defined once in a
file and turned into a C++ class at build time, following a fixed naming pattern: the type

The problem it solves is letting nodes exchange data without knowing about each other. A publisher doesn't know who is listening, or whether anyone is, and finding the other side of a topic is the middleware's job, a DDS implementation by default; a node can be restarted, replaced or never started at all, and the nodes on the other end of its topics keep running unchanged, noticing only through what does or doesn't arrive.
each return the one shared pointer that owns the publisher or subscription; the node itself keeps only a weak reference. A subscription's callback runs only while the node is

loops, waiting for work, and calls timer and subscription callbacks one at a time on the thread that called it, so a node that never spins receives nothing, and a callback that blocks stops every other callback on that node too.

The mistake that catches most first attempts is not keeping that returned pointer: if it isn't stored in a member, the publisher or subscription is destroyed at the end of the statement that created it, with no error and nothing in the log, and a subscriber built this way compiles cleanly and never receives a message. The same holds for timers and services; every handle a node creates has to be kept alive in a member for as long as it needs to work.

You meet exactly this in the interview question itself, sketching a publisher whose timer callback builds and sends a message once a second, where the parts that matter are the publisher and the timer kept alive as members and the call to
that makes either one ever run.
